summaries.headline: SF Parents Push Back on AI Reading Tool
summaries.summary: Nearly 1,000 San Francisco Unified parents, teachers and community members signed a petition demanding restrictions on AI tools in classrooms, specifically targeting Amira Learning, an AI-based tutoring program used to teach reading skills to elementary students. The petition, organized by Tech In Check San Francisco, calls for banning generative AI tools and chatbots on student devices and discontinuing AI programs for core skill instruction, citing concerns over student privacy — including the collection of children's voice recordings — and potential dependence on the technology, despite a company-funded study showing reading gains. The pushback follows Los Angeles Unified's recent ban on student AI use, signaling that parent skepticism toward classroom AI tools is spreading across California districts even as vendors tout efficacy data.

summaries.headline: Bed-Stuy Educator Wins $200K for Financial Literacy Push
summaries.summary: Aaliyah Duah, a 23-year-old Bed-Stuy native, won a $200,000 David Prize — New York City's answer to the MacArthur "genius" grant — for Financial Revolutionn, the personal finance program she built as a college sophomore and now runs in more than 30 NYC schools across four boroughs. Duah uses familiar reference points like Roblox, sneakers, and iPhones to teach credit, interest, and retirement concepts, and is releasing a coloring book aimed at kids as young as three to build financial vocabulary early. Her recognition lands as New York state rolls out a new mandate requiring grades 5-12 to learn budgeting and money management this year, with K-4 requirements following next year, underscoring a broader shift toward treating financial literacy as foundational rather than elective.

summaries.headline: NYC Chronic Absenteeism Stalls at One in Three
summaries.summary: New York City's chronic absenteeism rate held flat at 33.5% for the 2025-26 school year, meaning one in three students missed at least 10% of school days, a figure still far above the roughly 25% rate seen before the pandemic. The city has responded by overhauling attendance policy in June and requiring every school to designate a school avoidance liaison this year, with new rules pushing schools toward attendance success plans, mentors, and mental health referrals for chronically absent students. Two years of stagnant numbers despite these interventions suggest the neediest students—including those experiencing homelessness—face barriers that standard school-level fixes haven't yet cracked.

summaries.headline: Chronic Absenteeism Fixes May Miss Root Cause
summaries.summary: District and industry efforts to curb chronic absenteeism have failed to move the national needle since pandemic-era school reopenings, with rates never rebounding to pre-pandemic levels despite years of targeted interventions. Ivory Toldson, chief of research for Concentric Educational Solutions, argues the K-12 field's conversation hasn't caught up to a deeper cultural shift in how families and students view school attendance, meaning many current solutions are addressing symptoms rather than the underlying change in mindset. If the industry keeps designing interventions around old assumptions about why students miss school, leaders may keep spending resources without closing the gap.

summaries.headline: Denver Board Orders Probe of Antisemitism Claim
summaries.summary: The Denver school board voted unanimously to hire an independent investigator into allegations that Vice President Monica Hunter called board member Amy Klein Molk a "Zionist bitch" in separate conversations with the board president and superintendent last December and January. Hunter denies the claim, which is the most serious among a broader set of allegations board President Xóchitl Gaytán raised this month against Hunter and member DJ Torres, both of whom have called the accusations false. The episode extends years of interpersonal conflict on a board already strained by tension with Superintendent Alex Marrero, who has publicly criticized board overreach and explored jobs elsewhere.

summaries.headline: NYC Cuts Student YouTube Access on School Devices
summaries.summary: New York City has blocked student access to YouTube on school-issued Chromebooks and iPads both in classrooms and at home, effective Sept. 9, with exceptions only for videos teachers assign directly through Google Classroom. The move follows City Council pressure just a day earlier and builds on Mayor Zohran Mamdani's broader tech policy that bars individual screen use before third grade, caps screen time at 30-45 minutes for grades 3-8, and bans student-facing generative AI tools through eighth grade. The shift marks a notable reversal for a department that previously left YouTube access up to individual principals, signaling that skepticism toward classroom technology has moved from parent advocacy into official policy.

summaries.headline: Unions Press Hochul to Reject School Choice Tax Credit
summaries.summary: Teachers unions and civil rights groups, including AFT President Randi Weingarten and the NAACP, publicly pressed New York Gov. Kathy Hochul to opt out of a federal tax-credit scholarship program set to take effect in January 2027, arguing it diverts resources to private schools that can turn away higher-need students. The program, created under the Republican-backed One Big Beautiful Bill Act, lets taxpayers claim a federal tax reduction for donations up to $1,700 to scholarship organizations that fund private tuition and tutoring, and Hochul signaled in May she intends to opt the state in despite the pushback. With Hochul facing reelection in November and many of these same groups backing her campaign, the standoff tests how much political leverage traditional public education allies retain against a federal school choice mechanism state leaders can't directly defund.

summaries.headline: Indiana Vouchers Shift Toward Higher-Income Families
summaries.summary: Indiana's Choice Scholarship program grew by about 4,000 students in 2025-26, reaching roughly 80,000 total, but the pace of growth has slowed for a second consecutive year even as universal eligibility rules approved in 2025 haven't yet taken effect. For the first time, more vouchers went to families earning over $100,000 than under that threshold, with recipients making more than $200,000 nearly doubling since 2023-24, from 3,700 to 7,000 students, while the majority of participants still have never attended public school. As Indiana moves toward fully income-blind eligibility this year, the data suggest the program is increasingly subsidizing private school choice for families who may not need financial assistance to access it, a trend district leaders and lawmakers will likely watch closely once the new rules take full effect.

summaries.headline: Colorado Launches Homebuying Aid for Educators
summaries.summary: Colorado's new Schools to Home program, launched July 1, gives first-time homebuyer assistance to teachers and other public school employees struggling to afford housing near the schools where they work. The state-funded initiative has already helped 85 people and expects to support about 125 home purchases with an average of $80,000 in assistance per home, a meaningful figure given that the average teacher salary is roughly $78,000 while the median home price in the state hit $550,000 in July. The program adds to a growing list of state and district efforts—including rent subsidies and tiny-home options—aimed at using housing support as a retention and recruitment tool amid persistent teacher shortages.

summaries.headline: Districts Chose Staffing Over Teacher Pay Raises
summaries.summary: School funding has climbed substantially over recent decades, but inflation-adjusted teacher salaries have stayed flat and even dipped in recent years as inflation surged. Rather than raising pay, districts funneled new money into hiring additional staff to serve growing student needs, widening the pay gap between teaching and other college-educated professions while remote-work perks make outside fields more attractive. With teacher turnover rising and fewer young people entering the profession, district leaders face a reckoning over whether staffing growth was the right tradeoff against a compensation gap now driving people out of classrooms.

summaries.headline: A Presentation Remote Built to Reduce Distraction
summaries.summary: Presentation remotes have long served as glorified slide advancers, but Logitech's Spotlight 2 adds features aimed at keeping instructors focused on students rather than their tech. A hands-on review found its haptic feedback confirms button presses without requiring a glance at the screen, while built-in digital spotlighting, highlighting and magnification tools let presenters direct attention without relying on a traditional laser pointer. For instructional staff who present regularly, small design choices like these can determine whether technology fades into the background or keeps pulling focus away from the room.

summaries.headline: India Education Summit Targets AI, Mental Health
summaries.summary: The Schools of India Education Summit 2026 will convene educators, policymakers, and AI/EdTech specialists in Maharashtra from October 30 to November 1 to address emerging challenges in school education. Organizers have built the three-day agenda around practical, classroom-level strategies, with sessions covering AI's safe and responsible use, teaching methodology, school leadership, and student mental health, alongside an EdTech exhibition featuring smart classroom tools. The summit's focus on translating AI discussions into implementable classroom practice, rather than abstract policy debate, signals a broader shift toward grounding education technology conversations in day-to-day instructional realities.

summaries.headline: CTA Sues California Over $6 Billion in Withheld Funds
summaries.summary: The California Teachers Association, representing 310,000 educators, sued state officials this week over nearly $6 billion in education funding withheld through budget actions, arguing the moves violate the state's constitutional school funding guarantee. The suit targets $1.9 billion held back by Gov. Newsom in the 2024-25 school year and another $3.9 billion deferred in the Legislature's July budget revision, marking the second major legal challenge to Newsom's funding deferrals after the California School Boards Association's 2024 lawsuit, which remains ongoing alongside plans for a new filing next week. Districts already managing multimillion-dollar deficits and layoffs now face a widening legal fight over money they say is needed for counselors, class sizes, and mental health staffing — a dispute that could reshape how much fiscal flexibility the state has during future budget shortfalls.

summaries.headline: California Teachers Union Sues Over Funding Shortfall
summaries.summary: A California teachers union has filed suit against the state, alleging a $3.9 billion shortfall in school funding owed to districts. The legal action signals mounting friction between labor groups and state budget officials over how education dollars are calculated and distributed. For district leaders already navigating tight budgets, the outcome could reshape expectations around state funding commitments and set precedent for how shortfalls get litigated going forward.

summaries.headline: IPS Exits Shared Enrollment Platform, Charters Push Back
summaries.summary: Indianapolis Public Schools is dropping Enroll Indy, the citywide platform families have used for a decade to apply to both district and charter schools, in favor of shifting applications, lotteries, and registration into PowerSchool starting with the 2027-28 cycle that opens Nov. 5. Superintendent Aleesia Johnson framed the move as a cost-saver and a shift to a platform families already know, but charter leaders and Enroll Indy's board — made up of both IPS and charter representatives — quickly objected, with some questioning whether the change violates state law. The split comes just as a new mayor-appointed board with heavy charter representation is taking over key district and charter functions, raising the stakes for how enrollment access and coordination get decided citywide going forward.

summaries.headline: NY Ditches Regents Exams, Answers Lag Behind
summaries.summary: New York's Board of Regents voted to move forward with replacing Regents exams with a competency-based graduation system, even as state officials admit key implementation details remain unresolved. Current ninth, tenth, and eleventh graders will be the first cohorts affected by the change, but districts still don't know how they'll measure proficiency in core subjects like English and math under the new framework, with less than a year to prepare before the shift takes effect for the 2027-28 school year. EdTrust-New York has already called for a pause, and the gap between the state's ambitious timeline and the practical guidance schools need suggests districts may be left designing high-stakes graduation measures on the fly.

summaries.headline: Private Schools Push Out Voucher Students With Disabilities
summaries.summary: Families using disability-specific vouchers, like Ohio's Jon Peterson Special Needs Scholarship, are discovering that private schools can accept the funding and still dismiss students mid-year when their needs prove too costly or complex to serve. Annabelle Kelly, a 15-year-old with Rett syndrome, lasted three months at Cincinnati Christian Schools before staff told her grandparents — in a meeting that opened with a prayer — that her education exceeded what the school could provide, leaving the family scrambling for a new placement. Unlike public schools, which are bound by federal law to serve students with disabilities regardless of cost, private schools accepting voucher money generally face no such obligation, exposing a gap in accountability that leaves vulnerable families to absorb the risk when a "school choice" option turns out to be conditional.

summaries.headline: Kentucky Pushes Districts Past Surface Attendance Data
summaries.summary: The Kentucky Department of Education's research blog series on chronic absenteeism turns to what's actually driving the numbers, urging districts to look past attendance percentages toward the health, housing, and transportation barriers behind them. The third installment in the series points districts toward student well-being data and class-level attendance patterns as tools for spotting root causes — mental health struggles, housing instability, logistical gaps — rather than treating absenteeism as a single, undifferentiated metric. Framing attendance as a diagnostic signal rather than a compliance number gives district leaders a more actionable path than blanket interventions, especially as they design supports meant to reach specific families rather than entire populations.

summaries.headline: Judge Dismisses Data Privacy Suit Against Renaissance Learning
summaries.summary: A federal judge in California has dismissed a proposed class action against Renaissance Learning, the education software company, over claims it unlawfully collected and shared students' personal information. The court found the families' allegations insufficient to move forward, though the ruling's specific legal reasoning and whether plaintiffs can amend their complaint remain details district leaders will want to track. The case adds to a growing body of litigation testing how far ed-tech vendors can go in data collection practices before courts intervene, and a dismissal here may embolden similar platforms while leaving districts to make their own judgment calls on vendor vetting.

# Fiber Education and Digital Literacy Event

**Published on 9/16/2026**

**by**

Last updated: 9/16/2026 10:45 AM

Page Content

​​The Alachua County Broadband Initiative is hosting a free Fiber Education and Digital Literacy event on Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, from 10 to 11 a.m., at the Alachua County Senior Recreation Center (5701 NW 34th Blvd., Gainesville).

This event, in partnership with Kinetic, will focus on fiber broadband education, cybersecurity and digital literacy.

The program will introduce residents to fiber internet technology, essential technology skills and web-based tools that support everyday life at home, work and school. Participants will learn how to protect personal information online, recognize cyber scams, understand the benefits of fiber internet, and use digital tools more effectively.

This event is part of the Kinetic Digital Literacy Program, supported through the Alachua County Broadband Deployment Assistance Grant.

[View Kinetic's learning modules online](https://alachuacounty.us/news/Article/Pages/Fiber-Education-and-Digital-Literacy-Event.aspx#).

[Learn more about Alachua County’s Broadband Initiative](https://alachuacounty.us/Depts/OMB/broadband/Pages/default.aspx?_gl=1%2a19okrwy%2a_ga%2aMTI1NzgzODQ0LjE3ODIzOTkyOTU.%2a_ga_8BZDCPK2VM%2aczE3ODk1NjkwNTAkbzE2OCRnMSR0MTc4OTU3MDIxNSRqNDAkbDAkaDA.).

**HOOVER**— Jefferson State Community College invites the community to attend free artificial intelligence awareness and literacy training on Sept. 22 and 24.

The AI Community Caravan initiative, sponsored by the Alabama Community College System, is a statewide effort providing beginner-friendly workshops to learn the basics of artificial intelligence with the help of hands-on demonstrations and discussions led by experts.

The events are scheduled for:

This program is designed for beginners and will introduce participants to AI and its increasing role in everyday life and the workplace. Attendees will see live demonstrations, get answers to questions during interactive sessions and hear from panelists who will discuss practical uses of AI technology.

The workshops will also address common misconceptions and help dispel myths associated with AI.

“These two events are great opportunities for anyone to learn more about how AI is being used, and how it can help them in their work and everyday lives,” said David Bobo, Jeff State’s director of communication and marketing.

The Alachua County Broadband Initiative will host a free Fiber Education and Digital Literacy event on Friday, Sept. 25, at the Senior Recreation Center in Gainesville.

Courtesy Alachua County

Key Points

The Alachua County Broadband Initiative will host a free Fiber Education and Digital Literacy event on Friday, Sept. 25, at the Senior Recreation Center in Gainesville.

The event, held in partnership with Kinetic, will run from 10 to 11 a.m. at 5701 NW 34th Blvd. and will focus on fiber broadband education, cybersecurity and digital literacy.

Participants will learn about fiber internet technology, essential technology skills and web-based tools that support everyday life at home, work and school. The program will also cover ways to protect personal information online, recognize cyber scams, understand the benefits of fiber internet and use digital tools more effectively.

Residents can [view Kinetic’s online learning modules](https://alachuacounty.us/news/article/pages/Fiber-Education-and-Digital-Literacy-Event.aspx) and [learn more about the Alachua County Broadband Initiative](https://alachuacounty.us/Depts/OMB/broadband/Pages/default.aspx).

# Ohio proclaims ‘Dolly Parton Day’ to celebrate music icon and literacy pioneer

Ohio has proclaimed September 25, 2026, as Dolly Parton Day, honoring her contributions to childhood literacy and the statewide Imagination Library program.

By Kathy Laird September 16, 2026 8:30 am

![](https://marioncountynow.com/wp-content/themes/marioncountynow/screenshot.png)

COLUMBUS, OH ( [MARION COUNTY NOW](http://www.marioncountynow.com/))—In recognition of her global influence and extraordinary contributions to childhood literacy, Governor Mike DeWine and Lieutenant Governor Jim Tressel have officially proclaimed September 25, 2026, as Dolly Parton Day across the state of Ohio.

The official proclamation honors Parton’s journey from her humble beginnings in East Tennessee to her status as a worldwide icon whose music and philanthropy embody kindness, generosity, and community spirit.

At the center of the state’s tribute is Parton’s signature philanthropic initiative, the Imagination Library. Founded in 1995 to honor her father—who never learned to read—the program was created to foster a love of books among preschool children in her home county. Today, the global program mails more than 3 million free books every month to children from birth to age five.

Ohio has embraced Parton’s mission on a massive scale. Since the establishment of Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library of Ohio in 2019, the program has made every child in the state eligible to receive a free, high-quality, age-appropriate book in the mail each month.

When violist Matthew Consul visits kindergarten classrooms in Portland, he starts by playing a bit of music, asking students to close their eyes and “fully get into” the piece he’s about to play.

“Let your imagination take you away. See what comes up: emotions, stories, colors,” he tells them. Consul closes his eyes, too, but quickly opens them again so he can watch.

“Every year it blows me away, seeing them experience music with their entire being,” he said.

When he’s done playing, he asks what they felt.

One memorable response: “It made me feel sweaty,” along with “That music made me feel happy and expired, like milk.”

“I’ve been trying to figure that feeling out for almost a year,” Consul said, laughing.

Through the [PSO Explorers](https://portlandsymphony.org/education-community/youth-programs/pso-explorers/) program, Consul is one of several Portland Symphony Orchestra musicians who spend the school year with kindergartners through third graders at Longfellow Elementary School and Reiche Community School. Students have 30-minute sessions every other week, 16 times a year, with musicians dedicated to individual grade levels.

That consistency is a special part of the program. The musicians aren’t one-time visitors putting on a performance, but instead familiar faces whom students know and trust.

![](https://www.pressherald.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/09/Jan-2026_Explorers_by-SM-01-1-1.jpg?w=684)PSO violist Matthew Consul stands in front of a Reiche Community School kindergarten class with their teacher. He visits classrooms for 16 weeks of the year, using music to support the standard curriculum. _Photo courtesy Portland Symphony Orchestra._

“The students get to know the musicians really well, which gives them time to explore and develop meaningful connections,” said McKenzie Blanchard, director of learning and community impact at the PSO. “The Explorers program has become a pillar of what we do at the symphony. We are so lucky to be able to continue it year after year.”

While music education is a natural outcome of bringing professional musicians into the classroom, Explorers was designed differently from many school-symphony partnerships. Its goal is to use music to enhance what teachers are already teaching, with early literacy at its heart.

A centerpiece of the kindergarten curriculum in recent years has been “ [The Man With the Violin](https://kathystinson.com/books/picture-books/the-man-with-the-violin/),” by Kathy Stinson. It tells the story of a child who, while running errands with his busy mother, hears beautiful music in a subway station that the adults around him rush past. The story was inspired by violinist Joshua Bell’s real-life unannounced performance in a Washington, D.C., Metro station.

In her classroom, Reiche kindergarten teacher Amy Wu uses poster-size versions of the pages to return to the story over several weeks. Students explore the words, setting and sequence of events and connect the story to their own experiences, while Consul brings it to life through music.

Then the children get involved themselves, using percussion instruments such as drums, egg shakers and rhythm sticks to create sounds and respond to what they hear, or taking turns conducting the group, all lessons in cooperation and how individual actions can be more powerful in a group.

“Movement helps children gain knowledge through full-body experiences and engaging multiple senses,” Wu said. “So much of school is ‘sit and get,’ so to have this opportunity is so stimulating.”

That can be particularly helpful for English language learners. Wu also uses a small, colorful glockenspiel to gather students, signal transitions or provide a friendly countdown to an instruction. Wu said these sound cues are especially helpful for students who are learning English.

![](https://www.pressherald.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/09/IMG_2089.jpg)Reiche kindergarten teacher Amy Wu demonstrates how she uses her glockenspiel to gather students. _Photo by Molly Adams._

When young people are processing a new language all day, music, movement and visual cues offer other ways to understand and participate.

Wu has been involved with Explorers since its beginning in 2014, when Reiche teachers, led by now-retired music instructor Alyson Ciechomski, and PSO musicians worked together to develop the curriculum. The original team received a Yale Distinguished Music Educators Award in 2015.

More than a decade later, that teacher-musician collaboration remains central to the program’s success. Teachers provide regular feedback, the curriculum is continually evaluated and revised, and the PSO works continuously to better understand the program’s impact on students, teachers and musicians.

“To be successful, we have to keep centering educator voices in any education program,” Blanchard said. The PSO supports the program at no cost for schools, which goes beyond individual Explorers lessons and includes providing classroom materials and instruments. It is all funded thanks to grants and [donations](https://portlandsymphony.org/support/).

One measure of success is educational: Are students strengthening literacy skills, listening closely, sequencing stories and making connections between what they hear and what they read? But another is the social impact. Wu said kindergartners learn about community helpers and their own roles in the wider world. She said seeing professional musicians as people who live and work right here “is huge for them.”

Consul regularly hears cries of “MR. MATT!” when students spot him “in the wild” around Portland, and children will also recognize their Explorers musicians in the lobby or onstage at the [Magic of Christmas](https://portlandsymphony.org/event_type/magic-of-christmas/) or family [Discovery Concerts](https://portlandsymphony.org/education-community/discovery/) at Merrill Auditorium.

Some children become musicians themselves. Blanchard recalls one student who attended a PSO Discovery Concert as a child, fell in love with the violin and began taking lessons. She now plays with the Portland Youth Symphony Orchestra, which performs a side-by-side concert with the PSO every other year.

At the end of the school year, Consul has more than once found himself nearly knocked over by the force of a group goodbye hug. In Explorers, he sees everyday passion and joy as each child listens intently and becomes comfortable expressing what they think and feel.

For him, the goal is simple: “I focus on having fun, getting them excited and inspired,” he said. “Hopefully planting those seeds of passion and letting them flourish for themselves.”
